passage: On the back veranda of their house in Sydney, Xin sat with her journal on her knees, writing quickly: I hate that Mum read my message. I hate that I said I wished I could disappear for a weekend. Then she crossed out 'disappear' and wrote 'be alone'. Her sister Nadia knocked on the glass door and asked if she wanted tea. "Journal time," Xin said. Nadia nodded and put the mug on the step, and didn't look at the page. Later Xin read it back and felt calmer. The angry sentences were not plans, only feelings on paper. But one line, about feeling that nobody would notice if she stopped trying, made her pause. She folded the corner and thought of Mrs Chan, the school counsellor.

qa.q: Where was Xin sitting with her journal?
qa.a: She was on the back veranda of their house in Sydney.

qa.q: What did Xin realise when she read her journal back?
qa.a: She felt calmer and saw that the angry sentences were feelings, not plans. One line about nobody noticing worried her, which is why she thought of the counsellor.

qa.q: What should Xin do about the line that worried her?
qa.a: Share it with a trusted adult like Mrs Chan, since worries about safety are too big to hold alone, while keeping the rest of the journal private.

qa.q: How might Nadia's choice not to look at the page have felt to Xin?
qa.a: It probably felt respectful and caring, because she got privacy plus the tea.

grounding: A teen uses a journal as private space, writing is not acting, and a worry that touches safety is shared with a trusted adult.

passage: The hostel had a rule that the wardens never touched students' notebooks, and Anand had counted on that. In the evening quiet he wrote in his diary about missing home, about his father's cough and about feeling stupid in maths. Writing made the tightness in his chest ease. Disha, the counsellor, ran a weekly hour where students could write and keep their pages private. "You don't need to show me anything," she'd say. "But if something in there frightens you, please tell me or a trusted adult." One night Anand wrote about not wanting to get out of bed for a week. He sat for a while, then went to Disha's door. "There's something I need to say out loud," he said. She put the kettle on.

qa.q: What did the wardens never touch in the hostel?
qa.a: They never touched students' notebooks.

qa.q: Why did Anand go to Disha's door after writing about not wanting to get out of bed?
qa.a: He felt the feeling was too heavy to keep on paper alone, and he trusted Disha as an adult who respects privacy. He needed to say it out loud.

qa.q: What did Disha do that helped?
qa.a: She kept the writing private, invited students to tell her if something frightened them and put the kettle on when Anand came.

qa.q: How might Anand's father react if he knew Anand missed him?
qa.a: He may feel touched and worried, and want to call more often.

grounding: A teen uses a diary as private space, and a worry is shared with a trusted adult.

passage:
Dear Papa,
I found my diary moved on the shelf yesterday. I know you read it. I'm not shouting. I'm writing because I can say it better on paper.
That diary is where I sort myself out. When I wrote "I hate this family" last week, it was after the fight about my phone. I didn't mean I'd do anything. I was angry, I wrote it, and then I felt better and came down for dinner. Writing it is how I don't say it.
If you read it, I'll stop writing honestly, and then I'll have nowhere to put things.
I promise you this: if I'm ever worried about my safety, or someone else's, I won't keep it in a diary. I'll come to you or Mamma straight away.
Please let the diary be mine.
Sarika

qa.q: What did Sarika write in the diary after the fight about the phone?
qa.a: Sarika wrote "I hate this family."

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling on finding the diary moved?
qa.a: Sarika felt hurt and exposed that the private diary had been read, but tried to stay calm and explain.

qa.q: What makes Sarika's letter a good way to ask for privacy?
qa.a: It is calm, explains that writing angry words is not acting on them, and offers a clear promise to share any safety worry.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt reading "I hate this family"?
qa.a: Papa probably felt shocked and worried, which may be why he kept reading, not realising it was a way to let off steam.

grounding: The letter shows a teenager using a diary to sort feelings, asking for privacy, and promising to share safety worries with a trusted adult.

passage:
Aadhya, you asked how I, Lavanya, stay so calm. Honestly? A notebook.
Every night I write whatever's in my head. Mean things about my teachers. Crushes. Whether I'm pretty. Stuff I'd never say. Some nights I write "I'm quitting school" and in the morning I laugh and go.
Writing something down isn't a plan. It's just a place to put it.
But there was one time it was different. For a week I wrote about a man near my tuition who kept walking behind me and asking my name. I wrote it three nights in a row. On the fourth night I read those pages back and thought, this isn't a feeling. This is a safety thing.
So I went and woke my mother right then. She listened, told me I did the right thing, and the next morning she walked me to tuition and spoke to the tuition owner.
The notebook is private. But not for that.

qa.q: How many nights did Lavanya write about the man near tuition?
qa.a: Lavanya wrote it three nights in a row.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling on the fourth night?
qa.a: Lavanya felt worried and alarmed, realising the pages described a real safety concern, not just a passing feeling.

qa.q: Which choice of Lavanya's worked, and why?
qa.a: Going to wake the mother that night worked, because it turned a private worry into action, and the mother acted the next morning.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's mother have felt being woken with this?
qa.a: She was probably worried but relieved that Lavanya told her, and she responded calmly and protectively.

grounding: The spoken account shows a teenager using a private journal to sort feelings, and knowing that safety worries must be shared with a trusted adult.

passage:
I'm Jaya, Arnab's sister, three years older. This summer Arnab started carrying a small black notebook everywhere. He'd write on the terrace, at the dinner table, on the bus.
One afternoon he left it on the sofa. I'll be honest: I picked it up. I wanted to know if he was okay, because he'd been quieter since the fight with his best friend.
I held it for a whole minute. Then I put it down without opening it.
That evening I said, "You left your notebook out. I didn't read it."
He looked at me hard, then relaxed. "Thanks."
"If anything in there ever scares you, or you're worried about someone's safety, you'll tell me or Amma, right?"
"Yeah. It's mostly just me being annoyed."
A week later he read me one line he'd written about his friend. He chose it. That felt better than anything I could have read.

qa.q: What colour was Arnab's notebook?
qa.a: It was a small black notebook.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling while holding the notebook for a whole minute?
qa.a: Jaya felt worried about Arnab after the fight with his friend and tempted to read, but torn, because it would break his trust.

qa.q: What did Jaya get right?
qa.a: She respected his privacy, told him honestly, and made sure he knew to share any safety worry with her or Amma.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt if Jaya had read the notebook?
qa.a: He would probably have felt betrayed and might have stopped writing honestly or trusting her.

grounding: A sister's account shows respect for a teenager's private journal, with the understanding that safety worries should be shared.

passage:
Monday. After the fight over the cricket bat, Abhinav wrote in his notebook until his hand ached: I wish Omkar would just vanish for a year. He hid it under his mattress and felt calmer by dinner.
Wednesday. Omkar found the notebook while hunting for his charger, read that page and ran to Aai, half hurt, half triumphant. Abhinav's face burned. Aai read only the one line Omkar pointed to, then closed the notebook and handed it back. "Writing a feeling isn't doing it. This is yours. Omkar, you don't read it again." To Abhinav she added, "If something in there ever feels unsafe, bring it to me."
Saturday. Writing about the week, Abhinav noted that a player in his online game kept asking for his school name and had said, "don't tell your parents we chat." He stopped mid-sentence, stared at the line, then took the tablet to Aai. They blocked and reported the player together that evening.

qa.q: What did Abhinav write on Monday?
qa.a: Abhinav wrote: I wish Omkar would just vanish for a year.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when Omkar ran to Aai with the notebook?
qa.a: Abhinav felt exposed and ashamed, face burning, because a private angry line had been read; there may also have been fear of being taken literally.

qa.q: How did Aai balance privacy and safety?
qa.a: She read only the line shown, handed the notebook back, told Omkar not to read it again, and invited Abhinav to bring anything unsafe to her, which he did on Saturday.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt reading 'vanish for a year'?
qa.a: Omkar was likely hurt by the line, which is partly why he ran to Aai, even though it was only anger written down.

grounding: It shows a teenager using a private notebook to sort out feelings, a parent respecting that writing is not acting, and a safety worry being taken to a trusted adult.
